title: Camp 3 close: your week has a shape
hook: Shabbat, blessings, holidays, study: a life with rhythm

segments.voice: Yesterday, la'asok: be busy with the words of Torah. Your line was bless the words first. Today is the last day of this camp, a look back at all of it.

For a lot of people, a week goes like this. Monday blurs into Thursday. The weekend fills up with errands. Holidays sneak up and pass. It's a line with no shape, just more. This camp's sixty days began with a promise: I can do this. Not believe this. Do this. A candle, a cup, a blessing, a breath. Judaism answers the shapeless week with rhythm. Every day has its words, every week has its peak, every year has its seasons. Today, before a new camp begins, a walk back through what you've practiced, and a choice of what to keep.
screen: `I CAN DO THIS.` → `A WEEK WITH NO SHAPE.` → `A LIFE WITH RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: It started with Shabbat, holy time, not holy place. Erev Shabbat, getting ready as if a guest were coming. Candles, hands over the eyes. Kiddush over a cup. Two loaves of challah, covered. Melacha, the kinds of work set aside, and menuchah, real rest. The third meal at dusk, and Havdalah's braided candle and spices to carry the scent into the week. Then blessings through the day. Modeh Ani, thank you before you get up. Baruch, the word that opens almost every blessing. Hamotzi over bread, Birkat Hamazon after the meal, Shehecheyanu for firsts, and even a blessing inside grief. Then the year. The luach, a calendar kept by the moon. The shofar's cry, the sukkah's leafy roof, Hanukkah's lights, the seder's questions, counting the Omer to Shavuot. Tefillin on arm and head. Kosher, which means fit. And this last week: Talmud Torah, study as worship. Chavruta, learning in pairs. Kushya. Rashi on your shoulder. Hamaor shebah, the light inside it. La'asok. Look at the shape all that makes. The Torah itself begins it: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Six days of work, then a day that's different. Prayer at morning, afternoon and evening. A hundred small blessings, the Talmud says. Holidays that come back every year, so you meet yourself again. Nobody does all of it at once, and Jews keep these practices in very different ways. But a week can have a shape.
screen: `SHABBAT: CANDLES, CUP, TWO LOAVES.` · `BLESSINGS THROUGH THE DAY.` · `THE YEAR: SHOFAR TO SHAVUOT.` · `STUDY: PAIRS, QUESTIONS, RASHI.` · then, large: `THE WEEK HAS A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Let the camp pass in front of you: the candle, the cup, thank you before you get up, the blessing after a meal, a question at dinner, a study partner. Pick the three that felt like yours, one for each day, one for each week and one for the year. Hold them lightly; you can change them later.
Shavua. A week, from the word for seven: the shape sixty days of practice gave to Shabbat, blessings, holidays, tefillin, kashrut and study.
Your line: the week has a shape. Tomorrow a new camp opens the book at the center of it all: the Torah, one portion a week. Camp three, complete.

howItsDone: Jews shape the week around Shabbat, the day around prayer and blessings, and the year around the festivals; how many of these practices a person keeps varies widely across communities and families.

chat.says: How does Judaism keep a week from blurring together?
options: It gives time a shape: blessings daily, Shabbat weekly, holidays yearly.
It asks you to keep every practice at once, or none of them count.
It saves all the holiness for the big holidays, not the ordinary week.
chat.meaning: Six days, then Shabbat; blessings through the day; holidays that come back each year. Nobody does it all at once, but a week can have a shape.
